name: Gourmand fragrances

lead: Gourmand is a perfume style whose scents smell edible or dessert-like, typically using vanilla, tonka bean and coumarin, sometimes with synthetic notes that imitate food flavours. People choose them to add a warm, sweet signature to their grooming.

Fragrance is part of overall presentation: how someone smells is read alongside hair, skin and clothing. The wiki describes what the style is and how it is used; no studies are known that test gourmand scents specifically for attractiveness.

paras: Wearers apply the fragrance as an eau de parfum or similar spray as part of their routine. Perfume references note that scent behaves differently on different people: dry skin holds fragrance for less time, and spicy or fatty foods can intensify it.

Fragrance is a low-risk cosmetic, with the usual possibility of skin irritation or allergy for sensitive people. Sweet, heavy scents are often described as strong, so how much is applied affects how they are received.

angle.text: Users pick gourmands for a sweet, comforting signature scent that complements grooming. How it reads depends on the wearer's skin and how much is worn.

lead: Gourmand is a fragrance style in which scents have an edible or dessert-like character, usually built around vanilla, tonka bean and coumarin, and sometimes using synthetic materials that mimic food flavours.[1]

Perfume classification treats gourmand as a cross-cutting style rather than a strict family: broad groups such as floral, amber, woody and fresh sit alongside styles like gourmand and aquatic, and a family label is only a starting point for describing a perfume.[1]

In looksmaxxing, fragrance is one element of grooming and presentation. Gourmands are chosen for a sweet, warm impression, though no published research has tested this style on perceived attractiveness.

paras: Gourmand scents are defined by an 'edible' quality. Typical building blocks are vanilla, tonka bean and coumarin, with some perfumes adding synthetics that mimic food flavours.[1]

Vanilla comes from an orchid whose flowers must be pollinated and made into pods before use in perfumery, and it appears across both oriental and gourmand styles.[1] The oriental or amber class is described as sweet, slightly animalic scents based on ambergris or labdanum, often combined with vanilla, tonka bean, flowers and woods.[1]

Perfume references note that a wearer's physiology affects how a scent behaves: spicy and fatty foods can intensify fragrance, some medications change its character, and dry skin holds scent for less time.[1]
